item.title: Political Campaigns Are Quietly Paying Influencers to Support Candidates
item.description:
Josh Greene is a rising left-wing social media star with his own podcast, nearly 800,000 followers and access to politicians like Senator Bernie Sanders of Vermont and Mayor Zohran Mamdani of New York.

He has used that platform to support dozens of progressive candidates in the midterm elections, ranging from low-profile, down-ballot contests to some of the nation’s marquee Democratic primaries. In camera-facing videos, Mr. Greene informs his followers of his preferences, calling some candidates “the most viable” and, in other cases, declaring that “this is the candidate for you.”

He does not always tell his viewers that he is being compensated for his support.

But records show that Mr. Greene, 26, has received money from at least seven politicians, or outside groups supporting them, in the current campaign cycle, including several congressional candidates in New York and a super PAC linked to Dr. Abdul El-Sayed, the Senate nominee in Michigan. Tom Steyer, the former candidate for governor in California, paid him $21,500.

Mr. Greene, who lives in Southern California and is best known by his handle @joshtheprogressive, is among a growing number of influencers who, at a moment when campaigns are increasingly willing to pay for online attention, appear willing to put their mouth where the money is.

joshtheprogressive

🇺🇸 Political Commentator

joshtheprogressive

🇺🇸 Political Commentator

As more people spend time scrolling on their phones, campaigns view these shows of support from influencers as a vital way to reach voters. They are also significantly less expensive than traditional advertising.

But unlike campaign mailers, billboards and television spots, these messages fall into a legal gray area.

There are no federal regulations requiring disclosure of payments for political support on social media, and only a few states have such rules. That allows influencers, in most instances, to endorse candidates for a fee without ever disclosing those payments in their posts. Creators say some campaigns have even asked them to actively conceal the fact that they’re being compensated, making it impossible to know what’s genuine support — and what is pay-for-play.

In most cases, the only way a viewer would know an influencer is being paid would be to search a candidate’s campaign finance reports, as The New York Times did to discover the payments. Even then, such compensation is regularly obscured by funneling the payments through middlemen.

“It’s completely out of control,” said Suzanne Lambert, a progressive influencer and comedian with more than 1.3 million followers between TikTok and Instagram. She said that while she happily promotes candidates she likes, she has “never taken a cent” in exchange for an endorsement and worries that the practice distorts the democratic process. “People don’t know what’s real anymore,” she said.

Mr. Greene defended the idea of influencers getting paid for their work and noted that he accepts money only from candidates and campaigns that he would support anyway. “I turn down offers every single day because I’m not going to take money from any place if I don’t agree with it,” he said. (In the case of the Steyer campaign, Mr. Greene said he was initially critical but came to see him as the most viable candidate.)

Still, he suggested there was a need for straightforward and consistent rules on disclosure. “If anything, we do need more clear transparency laws so that creators like myself aren’t confused,” he said.

The phenomenon is bipartisan.

In June, Representative Barry Moore of Alabama filed a complaint with the Federal Election Commission, alleging that at least eight social media accounts were being paid to attack his military record during the Republican primary. In April, a newspaper in Kentucky revealed what appeared to be a coordinated network of influencers boosting Nate Morris — at the time running in a Republican Senate primary — even though none acknowledged being paid for their efforts. Ken Paxton, the attorney general of Texas and the Republican nominee for Senate, benefited from a paid campaign on X when he was facing impeachment in the state several years ago.

But the question of paid influence has gained particular attention in recent months thanks to aggressive efforts by a handful of Democratic candidates to secure support from well-known influencers.

During California’s hard-fought primary this spring, Mr. Steyer’s campaign paid 17 influencers at least $5,000 apiece, including one, Carlos Eduardo Espina, who has over 14 million followers on TikTok and received a total of $400,000, campaign finance filings show.

Former Representative Katie Porter, who also ran unsuccessfully for California governor, paid 12 influencers a total of $139,500. One of them, a lifestyle creator named Avery Cyrus with 9.5 million followers on TikTok, received $25,000 for what appeared to be a single post claiming “Katie Porter’s thing works.”

Ms. Cyrus’s post was deleted after The Times inquired about it. She did not respond to a request for comment made through the social media agency that represents her, UnderCurrent Media, but the firm’s chief executive, Eric Bogard, said in an email that it “was not asked to oversee disclosure compliance, nor were we provided instructions concerning any required disclosures.”

Under California law, paid political posts on social media must be disclosed. A Times review found three posts supporting Ms. Porter on TikTok from influencers who were paid by her campaign that did not include any disclosures. In seven other instances, the disclosures could be found only after clicking through to a hidden section of TikTok for comments flagged “as potentially offensive or disturbing.”

Sander Jennings, an influencer based in Florida who was paid $22,000, said “the Porter campaign and I agreed to disclose the payment” in TikTok’s comments section in order to get around the site’s practice of removing paid political posts. He said he did not know why the disclosures ended up in the hidden section of the comments.

TikTok’s terms of service bar all paid political advertising, including “creators being compensated for making branded political content. In an email, Ms. Porter said that “nothing was paid for and posted without review and coordination and compliance with all law.”

Other political efforts have employed a different strategy, contracting private firms that pay little-known content creators smaller sums to put out a large volume of posts. Those companies, known as user generated content platforms, or U.G.C.s, operate on the principle that carpet bombing the internet with hundreds of nearly identical posts is more likely to generate viral content than paying one large influencer the same amount of money to make a single post.

This spring, a woman posted dozens of videos promoting Mr. Steyer in the California primary. Weeks later, she appeared in videos from a different account complaining about the cost of living “here in Michigan” and encouraging people to vote for Representative Haley Stevens, Dr. El-Sayed’s primary opponent in the Senate race. Then she pivoted to a third account talking about affordability in Wisconsin.

Corporate records show that the woman, Paige Dunmeyer, actually lives in Kansas City, Mo., and is registered to work with a U.G.C. company called SideShift. It’s not clear how much she was paid for her Michigan and Wisconsin videos, but she has earned more than $30,000 on SideShift for a variety of political and commercial campaigns, according to company records reviewed by the Times. Filings from Mr. Steyer’s campaign showed she received $1,320 for her efforts in that race. Ms. Dunmeyer did not respond to requests for comment.

The Times identified her as a freelance content creator based in Kansas City, Mo.

Michigan

oakley.marie13

25 Wisconsin ☀️

A Times analysis found that at least 87 people registered to work with SideShift had made posts boosting Mr. Steyer or Ms. Stevens, or participated in a third campaign to post video clips on TikTok supporting Representative James Talarico, the Democratic Senate nominee from Texas. Most of the posts by those creators included no acknowledgment that money changed hands.

In a statement, SideShift said that it advises creators to follow applicable disclosure requirements, and called for more explicit laws governing how paid content is disclosed on social media.

“SideShift believes anyone can be a creator and that creators should get paid fairly for work they choose to do,” the company said.

In June, Kendall Boyle, a TikToker in Michigan with over 21,000 followers, was contacted by a social media marketing agency called Activate HQ offering her a paid opportunity to post videos about “how rising costs are affecting Michigan residents in real life.”

When she asked who was footing the bill, she was told it was Majority Forward, a dark money group linked to the Senate Majority PAC, a Democratic super PAC, email correspondence reviewed by The Times shows. Ms. Boyle said she was turned off by warnings in those emails from Activate HQ that “disclosure is not required and the paid partnership label will not be included in any posts” and also that Majority Forward “will not be mentioned” in her content.

“It was one of those things where something isn’t fitting right,” Ms. Boyle said.

In a statement, Majority Forward said the language in the email “explains disclosure requirements necessary under F.E.C. rules, which were fully followed.”

Just four states have laws or regulations requiring influencers to disclose paid political messaging, but they apply only to state and local races, not federal contests. Although regulations for social media have been proposed multiple times to the F.E.C., it has never taken action. The Federal Trade Commission, which requires disclosure of paid commercial content on social media, makes an exception for political messaging.

Representative Mark Takano, a California Democrat, introduced a bill in June that would require anyone paid by a candidate or political committee to clearly disclose that fact in the same way that traditional campaign materials are required to note such payments.

In an interview, Mr. Takano said he was inspired to draft the legislation after online sleuths revealed that numerous influencers had been making paid endorsements in the California governor’s race without proper disclosure, as required in that state.

“It’s unfair when an influencer is allowed to be silent or not transparent about money they’re taking from a candidate, making it seem like what they’re saying is authentic and not influenced by money,” he said.

Mr. Takano acknowledges that there are some potential loopholes in the bill. For instance: Campaigns often obscure payments to influencers by hiding them under layers of vendors and sub-vendors.

Ms. Porter, for example, hired Activate HQ for “influencer marketing services,” and it in turn paid 13 different creators to bolster her campaign for governor. One of them, a political influencer in Los Angeles named Dash Dobrofsky, who also posted in support of Ms. Stevens in Michigan, received $15,500 from Ms. Porter’s campaign. Mr. Dobrofsky did not respond to a request for comment.

He was paid $15,500 by her campaign.

Dash Dobrofsky

Author of The Gen Z Perspective

Dash Dobrofsky

Author of The Gen Z Perspective

Mr. Steyer’s campaign, for its part, hired multiple digital strategy firms to manage social media, including one called Group Project, which hired a Los Angeles company, Gutsy Media, which paid Mr. Greene through UnderCurrent, which represents him.

Those payment chains are visible because California is one of a handful of states that require campaigns to report payments to sub-vendors. There is no such obligation for campaigns for federal office. “Every dollar spent by this campaign is publicly disclosed and available for anyone to see,” the Steyer campaign said in a statement.

Occasionally, campaigns or independent expenditure groups will reveal direct payments to influencers, such as the super PAC Freedom PA, which supported the socialist candidate Chris Rabb’s successful bid to win a Pennsylvania House primary in May. It has disclosed payments to nearly 50 influencers for “social media consulting,” among them Mr. Greene, who received $750 and posted a video celebrating the candidate’s victory.

Other committees listing payments to Mr. Greene in federal filings employed less illuminating descriptions. Chuck Park, who unsuccessfully ran for Congress in Queens, N.Y., this year, listed a $300 disbursement to Mr. Greene as “staff salary.” Mr. Greene posted at least five videos promoting Mr. Park, none of which state that he had received payment.

Mr. Park, in an interview, said that Mr. Greene was in fact not employed by the campaign, but said that “our campaign absolutely leaned into new media” and that he spent time with Mr. Greene in Queens filming a series of videos.

Mr. Greene disclosed being paid on three of his posts about Mr. Steyer and told the Times that those videos were the only ones that he was specifically contracted by the Steyer campaign to produce. He said he didn’t receive compensation for prior posts about the candidate.

Mr. Greene has also supported Senator Ed Markey, the Massachusetts Democrat in a competitive primary against Representative Seth Moulton, and last month, he posted a video accusing Mr. Moulton of “posturing to be someone they really aren’t.” He posted a second video this month critiquing Moulton, this time for taking corporate political money.

Neither video includes disclosures and F.E.C. filings don’t show any payments to Mr. Greene related to Mr. Markey’s re-election bid. But a spokesman for Commonwealth Together, a super PAC that is supporting Mr. Markey, said it had paid Mr. Greene $3,500 for “digital communications consulting” through his agency, UnderCurrent.

Mr. Greene, in a text message, acknowledged the payment to support Mr. Markey, saying he took it because “because I believe he is by far the more progressive candidate in the race.”

The murkiness has left some in the political world uneasy. Last month Rynn Reed, the founder of Creator Congress, an organizing hub for influencers interested in politics, introduced a code of conduct for the group that would require creators to make clear when they’re paid, whether required by law or not.

“With no standards,” Ms. Reed said, “there’s going to be a race to the bottom.”

item.title: The Delight of San Francisco’s Dahlias
item.description:
The flowers seem stolen from a storybook, with pink pompoms sprouting next to flame-colored orbs and lavender pinwheels. In one of San Francisco’s oldest gardens, a group of summer camp children recently squealed as they marveled at rings of yellow petals larger than their heads.

Throughout the late summer months, eyes widen and phone cameras click as visitors delight in the dahlias of San Francisco.

“It’s hard to believe they’re real sometimes,” said Deborah Dietz, 75, as she got on her knees to inspect a petite purple blossom in the Dahlia Dell, the garden that is in Golden Gate Park.

Compared with roses and orchids, dahlias are far wilder and more varied, appealing to lovers not of perfection but of wonder. And they have captured San Francisco’s imagination for generations.

In the early 1900s, the city built a reputation as one of the best places in the world to grow dahlias, which are native to Mexico. There were yearly dahlia competitions at the gilded Palace Hotel, where a prized tuber could sell for as much as $15, then equivalent to three days’ wages.

The San Francisco Board of Supervisors in 1926 named the dahlia the city’s official flower, celebrating its hardy nature, immigrant roots and unmatched “gayety and color.”

“In its versatility, its beauty, its infinite variety of color and form, it is the very symbol of San Francisco life and of the spirit of her people,” the proclamation reads.

That was long before televisions, jet engines or smartphones, and in the hundred years since, San Franciscans moved on to other pursuits. Yet, in today’s world of doomscrolling, climate anxiety and A.I. uncertainty, dahlias are once again en vogue.

Timothy Wong, 37, began growing dahlias in San Francisco six years ago and now spends more hours than he will admit with his hands in the dirt. His friends have been inspired by him to raise them, too, and he has noticed a younger crowd beginning to attend the local dahlia society’s tuber sales and annual show.

“Flower farming is everyone’s dream escape from daily life now,” said Mr. Wong, who recently started a popular new dahlia garden in the city.

In the early 1900s, several commercial dahlia growers operated in the western half of San Francisco when it was still just sand dunes. Later, families planted dahlias in the backyards of the narrow homes built in what came to be known as the Sunset and Richmond districts adjacent to Golden Gate Park.

Dahlias are originally from the highlands of Mexico, so they struggle in many parts of the United States with extended freezes or temperatures exceeding 85 degrees. They thrive, however, in the well-draining soil and cool weather of the Bay Area, where climate extremes are tempered by maritime fog.

“A lot of people think San Francisco’s a pretty nice place to live — a lot of plants think that, too,” said Isaac Lichter Marck, a plant ecologist who studies the sunflower family, which includes dahlias, at the California Academy of Sciences.

Dahlias peak in August and September and don’t wither until late fall, with an internal clock left over from when they would bloom after late summer monsoons in Mexico, Mr. Lichter Marck said. The unique timing is another reason gardeners love them — they blossom just as other summer flowers wind down their annual show.

On a recent afternoon at the Dahlia Dell, a man set up a folding table in the shade, facing the flowers. He dipped his brush in a watercolor kit.

“For dahlias, there’s nothing in the world like this,” said Kevin Woodson, a painter who splits his time between Taiwan and Oakland, Calif.

Dahlias have been grown in Golden Gate Park since the 1880s, and the dell is currently tended by seven volunteers, each of whom is assigned a section to plant and take care of. Dahlia varieties have names as whimsical as their forms, including Kung Fu Kitty, Fuzzy Wuzzy, Boogie Nites and I’m a Hottie.

The flowers’ unusually high number of chromosomes allows them to pull off a kind of botanical magic trick, transforming a dahlia garden into what appears to be a riot of different flowers in all shapes and sizes. Sarah Smith, 60, cupped in her palm a bloom resembling a pink-and-white daisy. Next to her was a dahlia with flowers that mimicked red carnations.

Ms. Smith, a retired third-grade teacher who lives in the Sunset District, recalled getting hooked on dahlias about five years ago when she became responsible for her own patch in the dell. Tending to the plants felt like a respite from a world that increasingly divided one’s attention, she said.

“Looking at every stem, every leaf, every bud, every everything, and the hours would just fly by, and it was so therapeutic to just be in that space,” she said. “It’s the opposite of sitting in front of a screen.”

The culture around dahlias often involves sharing plants and growing tips, and distributing stunning cut flowers. Ms. Smith and other dahlia fans said they saw it as an antidote to San Francisco’s reputation these days as a cradle for tech companies minting billionaires.

At the Dahlia Dell, bakers, doctors and file clerks alike donate their time to create something beautiful for the public to enjoy at no cost.

Ms. Dietz, a retired pharmaceutical sales representative who has been planting dahlias in the dell for more than 30 years, shows her flowers at the city’s annual dahlia competition every August. It is the floral equivalent of a Westminster Kennel Club Dog Show, where blooms are judged on countless characteristics such as petal shape, stem stiffness and leaf size. With a gloved hand, she touched the small rosy petals of Elvira, one of her favorite dahlias, which she called “the most beautiful Chihuahua at the show.”

Ms. Dietz welcomes a few volunteers each year who want to learn how to care for the flowers. Dahlias force one to work at their speed, and there’s something that feels right about getting down in the dirt with them, she said.

As Ms. Dietz gardened at the Dahlia Dell, a tourist fed her Labrador treats to get him to sit in the exact right position to photograph beside the brightest pink blossoms.

Another woman walked past the garden, distracted by her phone. Then she stopped abruptly. She turned, looked over and just stared at the dahlias.

item.title: How a California Bill Sparked a MAGA-Sphere Uproar
item.description:
The bill began as an effort to protect immigration aid workers, who said they were increasingly fearful of being doxxed and threatened as immigration raids swept through California last summer.

Democratic state lawmakers presented it as a simple expansion of a longstanding program, Safe at Home, that had shielded the addresses of vulnerable residents in public records. Many states created such programs in the 1990s to protect survivors of domestic violence or stalking victims. Over the years, some states expanded the programs to include abortion-clinic workers or law enforcement officers.

In California, such expansions never became free speech controversies. Last year, the state added health workers who provide gender-related treatment to the list, with little hubbub.

It wasn’t until state lawmakers moved this year to include immigration aid providers that a firestorm ignited. And that largely occurred after a Republican opponent of the bill gave it a catchy nickname: “The Stop Nick Shirley Act.”

Mr. Shirley, 24, has quickly become a hero in the MAGA movement as a YouTube influencer whose viral videos claimed to expose fraud in Democratic-led states. His videos last year on Minnesota child care centers run by Somali immigrants caught the attention of President Trump, who was cracking down on illegal immigration in the state. Soon after, Mr. Shirley made his way to California, where he recorded videos outside the homes of licensed child care providers, most of whom were immigrants, and the offices of hospice care providers.

Mr. Shirley has focused on fraud, and Republicans have mostly attacked the bill on free speech grounds, saying that it would prevent problems from being exposed. But immigrant aid groups have faced criticism from supporters of Mr. Trump because they provide everything from food to legal aid to the undocumented residents who have become especially vulnerable to deportation in the president’s second term.

The California bill this year was the first in the nation to expand address protection to workers and volunteers for immigration support services who face threats of violence or harassment. It says that, starting in October 2027, a person whose address is protected can sue someone who posts their image or personal information online after being asked in writing not to share it publicly.

Democrats say the bill only restricts people from posting violent threats with the intent to do imminent harm. Mia Bonta, the Bay Area assemblywoman who introduced the bill, said it was “150,000 percent absolutely not” inspired by Mr. Shirley. A spokeswoman for Gov. Gavin Newsom, who signed it into law last week, argued that it would have no impact on the conservative influencer.

But Mr. Shirley and his supporters argue that the bill was written to deter him from posting videos about what he says is fraud in social service programs for immigrants. In particular, they take issue with the provision allowing aid workers to sue.

Mr. Shirley, who has nearly 2 million YouTube subscribers and an online merch shop he calls the “Anti Fraud Club,” has turned fighting the new law into a cause célèbre, drawing national attention to what might otherwise be an obscure piece of legislation. Through viral video clips, appearances on Fox News and a rally this week at the State Capitol that attracted hundreds of people, Mr. Shirley has helped Republicans reframe the address bill into an argument over exposing fraud and protecting free speech.

“Welcome to the Cali-fraudia Republic,” Mr. Shirley said as he stepped to the microphone at the rally on Wednesday in Sacramento. “Here in California, the politicians, instead of going after the fraudsters, they’ve now gone after those that are going to expose the fraud.”

For a few hours, the plaza outside the State Capitol had the feel of a MAGA street fair, with booths selling Charlie Kirk-themed T-shirts and posters celebrating ICE officers. Trumpets and drumming blared from masked counterprotesters that the police kept on the perimeter of the event after a fistfight broke out during the rally’s opening prayer. (Three people were detained, according to the California Highway Patrol.)

Mr. Shirley began speaking after the crowd chanted, “Nick! Nick! Nick!” He was joined on stage by several Republican lawmakers and candidates. Numerous speakers said they looked forward to the law being overturned in court.

In an interview after the rally, Mr. Shirley said it was a “lie” that the bill was not directed at him. He said there was no need for the new law because it’s already illegal to dox people and make violent threats.

“They’re making a protected class by specifically saying ‘immigration support service providers,’” he said.

Mr. Shirley said he worried that the law could be used against him by people who hire someone to commit a crime and say they were incited by him.

“Then Nick Shirley is responsible,” he said, and, under the law could have to pay a fine of at least $4,000.

In California, recent expansions of Safe at Home have generally gone to groups aligned with Democrats, who control the state legislature. Democrats argue that these workers have been most targeted through doxxing by opponents.

But it is not clear what the threshold should be, and courts could ask how California has decided certain groups deserve a higher level of privacy. Eugene Volokh, a First Amendment scholar at the University of California, Los Angeles, School of Law, thought the bill could be vulnerable to challenge for protecting one group over another.

“It might be the case that a court would say this is unconstitutional because it specially protects immigration service providers,” Mr. Volokh said. He added that a court could rule that “you can’t single out threats and incitement against immigration service providers from threats and incitement against other people who might be just as vulnerable as they are.”

Early versions of the bill included broader prohibitions on posting information that free speech advocates said would have violated the Constitution. But the bill was later narrowed.

Carolyn Iodice, legislative and policy director with the Foundation for Individual Rights and Expression, a group that promotes free speech, was among those who criticized the bill in its early stages. She said the final version shouldn’t inhibit Mr. Shirley.

“The way I read it now is, unless he posts videos with threats or incitement, which is a very high bar, he should not face liability under the bill,” Ms. Iodice said.

However, she said, the law could wind up chilling some speech because people who receive legal demands that they not post images or information may not know that they are only prohibited from making comments that threaten or incite violence.

Immigration service providers who sought the new law said they have been facing intense harassment since Mr. Trump began his second term in office.

“We are an enemy that they feel is their patriotic duty to go after,” said Angelica Salas, executive director of the Coalition for Humane Immigrant Rights of Los Angeles, which worked with Ms. Bonta to develop the law.

Ms. Bonta, who is married to Rob Bonta, the state attorney general, said her bill was inspired by stories of fearful encounters. Ms. Salas said that someone showed up at her mother’s home looking for her.

Ms. Bonta said the law would not stop Mr. Shirley from making videos or inhibit journalists from covering groups supporting immigrants. She said her bill had been misrepresented by opponents who attached it to Mr. Shirley and that he was “not being honest with his viewers.”

“I am greatly disappointed that our legislative process can be so ambushed, if you will, by ill-intended legislators and people who are likely wanting to get more clicks for their own personal gain,” she said.

Online, many of Mr. Shirley’s followers seemed to believe “Stop Nick Shirley Act” was the bill’s formal title.

Carl DeMaio, the Republican assemblyman who came up with the moniker, said that he had never talked to Mr. Shirley when the nickname occurred to him during a committee hearing this spring. Invoking a popular figure helped him draw attention to his concerns.

“It’s the best way to simplify the scheme that they’re trying to hide,” he said.

“A bad bill needs public transparency, and I’m not going to apologize for that.”

item.title: Dolly Inspired Their Wigs and Makeup, and Had Their Back, Too.
item.description:
A drag performer named Brigitte Bandit, in a pink wig and with a full face of makeup, told Texas lawmakers that her art form should be celebrated, not treated as a threat to young people. She read from a children’s book by Dolly Parton, who wrote about how she thought her big hair and makeup made her beautiful and that others did, too.

Brigitte’s plea that day in 2023 did not change the minds of the legislature’s Republican majority. The bills she had spoken out against, including one that essentially aimed to criminalize performing drag in front of minors, passed by wide margins.

Still, one very important person had noticed: Dolly Parton.

Not long after, Brigitte was handed a pink box during a performance. Inside was an acoustic guitar adorned with rhinestones and Ms. Parton’s loopy autograph.

“All of that was very hard,” recalled Brigitte, whose name offstage is Cheri Lake. “To know that she recognized that and acknowledged that in such a powerful gesture was incredibly meaningful.”

That was Dolly, many in the L.G.B.T.Q. community said, as they grieved her death on Tuesday at age 80. Even if they had never met her, they felt they knew her well enough to call her by her first name, and that she knew and understood them, too.

That understanding counted for quite a bit, especially in parts of the country where conservative legislative efforts in recent years have compounded a long history of gay, lesbian and transgender people being marginalized and misunderstood.

On most issues, Ms. Parton steered herself away from the country’s political divisions, casting herself as an entertainer, and not a partisan figure. Yet, her advocacy and embrace of the L.G.B.T.Q. community was a rare area in which she would willingly step into the fray, even if it meant opening herself up to criticism or risking her unusual position as a public figure who was so widely admired.

“She reminded us of who had our back,” said Brian Sullivan, a leader in Nashville for the Tennessee Equality Project. “She wasn’t a pushover, and she certainly wasn’t when it came to us.”

One aspect of the mourning has been a recognition that the community had lost not only a powerful advocate but also a source of comfort and affirmation at a particularly uncertain moment.

In recent years, conservative lawmakers have pursued bills aimed at limiting drag performances in public spaces and what could be taught in public schools about sexual orientation and gender identity. Laws restricting gender expression and access to health care and public restrooms for transgender people have passed in dozens of states. Polls also showed that public support for gay marriage has slipped after years of strides toward acceptance for gay people.

“She left us, just at a hard time,” said Nadine Hubbs, a professor of women and gender studies and music at the University of Michigan.

Sometimes, Ms. Parton’s support came from being outspoken on issues such as gay marriage. Other times, it was from sly forms of acknowledgment, like when she said, “If I hadn’t been a girl, I’d have been a drag queen.”

She also produced “Common Threads,” a 1989 documentary about the AIDS Memorial Quilt; the Academy Award-winning film was credited with humanizing the crisis and its victims for a mass audience.

“She stood up for the right things and showed what it means to care for people who are different from you in real time,” said Bentley Hudgins, who is poised to become the first openly nonbinary and transgender person elected to the Georgia State Legislature, having been chosen by voters to be the Democratic nominee in the November election for a safe Democratic seat in the Atlanta area. “Through her authenticity, she showed how you can be confident and expressive and still be kind.”

Activists, researchers and others argued that Ms. Parton’s influence was not just a byproduct of her megawatt celebrity. They pointed to how she drew on her faith, leaning on Christian teachings and scripture to explain why she embraced L.G.B.T.Q. people and encouraged others not to pass judgment.

The stance prompted backlash among some Christian conservatives, who claimed that she was wrongly using her faith to justify behavior they condemned as immoral. But the criticisms gained limited traction.

Her ties to the L.G.B.T.Q. community brought her to glittery environs and gay meccas. She partied with Andy Warhol at Studio 54 and told interviewers over the years that she had once entered a Dolly Parton look-alike contest at a club in West Hollywood (she lost).

She loomed large even in establishments where she had never stepped foot, like CORE, a watering hole between an interstate and strip malls in Knoxville, Tenn.

Kelley Coulter, who sometimes tends bar there, added a tattoo of a haloed Ms. Parton on her thigh six years ago.

“She made everyone happy and feel at home,” Ms. Coulter said. She also served as a bridge, as a shared appreciation for Ms. Parton helped reduce the distance that otherwise existed with some loved ones.

For Ms. Coulter, that had been the case with her grandfather, she said. “That was the one woman that my pop loved more than anybody in the world,” she recalled.

Her grandfather — a “very old fashioned man” — played Ms. Parton’s vinyl records while he worked in his wood shop.

When Ms. Coulter came out to him as gay, a mutual love for Ms. Parton helped keep their relationship intact. Eventually he told her, “I don’t care who you love, as long as they respect you and they love you,” she said.

When he died three years ago, he left the records to her.

A 32-year-old transgender woman and drag queen in Atlanta who performs as Edna Allan Hoe (and is Edna Workman offstage) grew up in a conservative family and attended Christian schools. “I speak to my family, but not often,” she said. “But they did text me when Dolly Parton died.”

Ms. Parton’s death has been a reminder of her moral clarity, Professor Hubbs said, which allowed her “cut through the noise to see the core humanity of others.”

Her absence, she added, left a void that would be difficult to fill. “That is our task,” Professor Hubbs said. “I don’t know if anyone feels ready or up for that yet. We’re still processing our loss.”

Ms. Parton was helping with that, too. For some, it was listening on repeat to the songs that meant the most to them: “Coat of Many Colors,” one of Ms. Parton’s favorites, about her mother stitching together a garment for her out of rags. Or “Wildflowers,” where she sang “wildflowers don’t care where they grow.”

At Mary’s, a gay bar in Atlanta, the grieving began with a curated list of Ms. Parton’s songs and music videos on Tuesday night. On Wednesday, it was karaoke. And on Thursday, drag performers channeled the spirit of Dolly as best they could.

Edna performed “You Are,” a ballad that swells like the affection that Ms. Parton professes in the song as it moves along. Its lyrics encapsulated what she felt about Ms. Parton in that moment.

You are my thoughts when I’m awakeAnd my dreams when I’m asleepYou are the reason for my smileYou are the words I speak

On the day Ms. Parton died, a federal judge in Texas ruled against the law that Brigitte had spoken out against in 2023.

The judge found the law, which criminalized “sexually oriented performances” in the presence of minors, was unconstitutional and overly broad, extending to a range of performances that lawmakers may not have wanted to target with legislation.

He pointed to Ms. Parton as an example — “a voluptuous sex symbol,” he wrote, “because of her big hair, flamboyant clothes and breast exposure.”

On a day that had otherwise been consumed with loss, Brigitte said, she suddenly felt some relief, and even joy.

Emily Cochrane contributed reporting from Nashville.
